Gap: Applies only to large frontier developers (as defined in CA-SB53-22757-11); the required frontier AI framework addresses catastrophic-risk management, not a general organisational AI policy covering all AI development and use.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; website publication record; framework approval and compliance log
Rationale: Bus. & Prof. Code s.22757.12(a) requires large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and publish a frontier AI framework, which partly evidences a documented AI policy but only for a narrow class of developers and a catastrophic-risk scope.

Gap: Annual review duty applies only to large frontier developers and only to the frontier AI framework (catastrophic-risk scope); it does not cover a general AI policy or review on other changes beyond material modifications, which must be published with justification within 30 days.
Evidence_Examples: Annual framework review record; published modified framework with justification; review calendar showing the yearly cadence
Rationale: Bus. & Prof. Code s.22757.12(b)(1) requires large frontier developers to review and update the frontier AI framework at least once per year, which partly satisfies planned policy review but only for that narrow developer class and framework scope.

Gap: Only large frontier developers; the framework must describe the developer's approach to internal governance among its listed topics, but the Act does not require a defined organisation-wide AI role set with named owners.
Evidence_Examples: Frontier AI framework section on internal governance; internal role chart for frontier-model work; governance meeting records
Rationale: Bus. & Prof. Code s.22757.12(a) requires the frontier AI framework to describe how the developer approaches its listed topics including internal governance, which partly evidences defined AI responsibilities but only for large frontier developers.

Gap: Only covered employees (those assessing, managing or addressing critical-safety-incident risk) are protected, and only for catastrophic-risk or SB 53-violation disclosures: (a) anti-retaliation and no-gag protection binds all frontier developers, but the (e) anonymous internal process is large-developer-only. General AI concerns, other staff and contractors are outside it.
Evidence_Examples: Anonymous internal reporting channel record; monthly update to the reporter; quarterly disclosure summary to officers and directors
Rationale: Lab. Code s.1107.1(a) bars retaliation and rules, policies or contracts that prevent a covered employee from disclosing catastrophic-risk or SB 53-violation information, and (e) requires large frontier developers to provide an anonymous internal process for such disclosures, which partly satisfies a concern-raising channel but only for that narrow class and subject matter.

Gap: The frontier AI framework duty binds large frontier developers only, while the transparency report is owed by ALL frontier developers; both describe risk approaches, intended uses and restrictions, not a per-system inventory of all resources used.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; transparency report per frontier model; framework annual review records
Rationale: Section 22757.12 is the closest California counterpart because it requires large frontier developers to publish a documented framework and transparency reports, but its scope is frontier models only and it is not a resource inventory.

Gap: No California law in the inventory requires documenting the tools used to build, run or monitor AI systems; the SB 53 frontier AI framework covers catastrophic-risk approaches, not tooling.
Evidence_Examples: No artefact exists under this law; a voluntary tool inventory and build and monitoring tool records would evidence the control itself
Rationale: Section 22757.12 is the closest related requirement because it is California's broadest AI documentation duty, but its contents concern risk management, not tools, so there is no counterpart.

Gap: SB 53 reaches only frontier developers: §22757.12 requires large frontier developers (as defined in CA-SB53-22757-11) to publish a frontier AI framework addressing catastrophic-risk assessment and management, while §22757.13 incident reporting applies to ALL frontier developers — the $500M qualifier attaches only to the framework duty, not to incident reporting. The Act addresses catastrophic risk to public safety only, not wider societal effects, and only for models trained with more than 10^26 operations.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; catastrophic-risk assessment records; critical safety incident reports to CalOES
Rationale: SB 53 is California's only society-scale impact lens — catastrophic risk, defined in §22757.11(c) as a foreseeable, material risk of death or serious injury to more than 50 people or more than $1B in property damage or loss from a single incident, via three mechanisms (assistance with weapons of mass destruction, unsupervised cyberattack or violent-crime conduct, evading control), subject to stated exclusions — but its frontier-only scope and catastrophic-risk-only subject leave ordinary societal impacts of AI systems entirely unassessed.

Gap: Only large frontier developers (as defined in CA-SB53-22757-11) must publish a frontier AI framework; it covers catastrophic-risk thresholds and mitigations, not general responsible-development objectives, and all other AI developers are outside its scope.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework (s. 22757.12(a)); catastrophic-risk threshold definitions; annual framework review record
Rationale: SB 53 s. 22757.12 is the only California duty that requires a developer to publish documented objectives-like commitments for frontier models, so it partially covers A.6.1.2 for a narrow class of developers only.

Gap: SB 53 s. 22757.12 requires a frontier AI framework covering catastrophic-risk assessment, mitigations and incident response, but it does not require documented processes for responsible design and development across the AI lifecycle, and it applies only to large frontier developers. The (a)(3)-(a)(4) deploy-decision review is assessment and mitigation review for frontier models, not a design and development process standard.
Evidence_Examples: Frontier AI framework (shows the gap: risk framework, not a design/development process standard); lifecycle procedure (to show what the law does not require)
Rationale: SB 53's framework duty is risk- and frontier-focused, not a general lifecycle-process duty, so it does not satisfy A.6.1.3 even for covered developers.

Gap: SB 53 s. 22757.12(c) requires a transparency report before/concurrently with deploying a new or substantially modified frontier model, covering intended uses and restrictions, but this is a publication duty for frontier developers only, not a requirements-specification process.
Evidence_Examples: Transparency report for the model release; intended-use and restrictions statement; release checklist
Rationale: The transparency report's intended-use and restriction content is the closest California analogue to a documented requirements specification, limited to frontier models.

Gap: SB 53 s. 22757.12 requires large frontier developers to publish a frontier AI framework and transparency reports, but these describe risk approaches and model-release facts, not the design and development choices behind a system, and they apply only to frontier developers.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; transparency report for the model release; catastrophic-risk assessment summary
Rationale: The SB 53 framework and transparency report document some development-relevant decisions for frontier models, which partially overlaps A.6.2.3 within a narrow scope.

Gap: SB 53 s. 22757.12 requires a large frontier developer's framework to cover catastrophic-risk thresholds and assessments and third-party assessment, but this is assessment of catastrophic risk for frontier models only, not general verification and validation of an AI system against defined criteria.
Evidence_Examples: Catastrophic-risk assessment summary; third-party evaluator engagement record; framework review record
Rationale: The SB 53 assessment duties are the closest California analogue to validation (independent assessment against thresholds), limited to catastrophic risk for frontier developers.

Gap: SB 53 s. 22757.12(c) requires a frontier developer to publish a transparency report before or concurrently with making a new or substantially modified frontier model available to a third party, but this is a publication precondition for frontier models only, not a deployment plan or release-readiness confirmation.
Evidence_Examples: Transparency report published at release; release checklist showing publication timing; model version record
Rationale: The transparency-report timing duty is a pre-deployment publication gate for frontier models, which partially overlaps the release-confirmation element of A.6.2.5.

Gap: SB 53 s. 22757.12 requires large frontier developers to publish a frontier AI framework and transparency reports, but these are public risk and release documents for frontier models only, not the technical documentation each relevant party needs for an AI system.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; transparency report for the model release
Rationale: The SB 53 framework and transparency report are the closest California public-documentation duties for frontier models, which partially overlap A.6.2.7 within a narrow scope.

Gap: SB 53 s. 22757.13 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the California Office of Emergency Services within 15 days (24 hours to an appropriate authority if imminent risk of death or serious injury), which presupposes event records, but it imposes no general event-logging duty and applies only to frontier developers.
Evidence_Examples: Critical safety incident report to Cal OES; incident discovery and triage log
Rationale: The s. 22757.13 incident-reporting duty is the closest California logging-adjacent duty: it requires timely reporting of defined safety incidents, which implies event records, but it does not require logging decisions or log retention generally.

Gap: Section 22757.13 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the California Office of Emergency Services within 15 days of discovery (24-hour disclosure to an authority with jurisdiction where there is imminent risk of death or serious injury), but only for frontier models and only for the narrowly defined critical safety incidents in Sec. 22757.11(d); there is no general external problem-reporting channel.
Evidence_Examples: Critical safety incident reports to Cal OES; 24-hour imminent-risk disclosures; incident-discovery and triage log
Rationale: Section 22757.13 is the closest California analogue because it sets a deadline-driven reporting obligation for AI system problems, but it is confined to frontier developers and critical safety incidents, so it covers only a small part of A.8.3.

Gap: Section 22757.13 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to Cal OES within 15 days of discovery and to disclose imminent-risk incidents to an authority with jurisdiction within 24 hours, but only for frontier models and the narrow critical-safety-incident definition; it does not require a documented plan for communicating incidents to customers, users, or other affected parties.
Evidence_Examples: Critical safety incident reports to Cal OES; 24-hour imminent-risk disclosures; incident triage log recording discovery date and recipient
Rationale: Section 22757.13 is the closest California analogue because it sets recipients and deadlines for communicating defined incidents, but it is confined to frontier developers and critical safety incidents, so it covers only part of A.8.4.

Gap: Section 22757.12 requires large frontier developers to write, implement, comply with and clearly and conspicuously publish on their website a frontier AI framework describing how they approach catastrophic-risk management, with annual review and publication of material modifications within 30 days, but it binds only large frontier developers (as defined in CA-SB53-22757-11) and covers framework publication, not general information sharing with interested parties.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework on the developer website; annual review records; material-modification publication notices with justifications
Rationale: Section 22757.12 is the closest California analogue because it requires public sharing of defined AI-system information with interested parties, but it is confined to large frontier developers and to the framework document, so it is Partial.

Gap: Applies only to large frontier developers (as defined in CA-SB53-22757-11); the framework describes the developer's approach to catastrophic-risk topics, not documented objectives guiding the responsible use of AI systems generally.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; annual framework review record; pre-deployment transparency report
Rationale: Section 22757.12 requires large frontier developers to publish a framework describing how they approach catastrophic-risk assessment, mitigation and related topics, which functions as a documented statement of approach, but for a tiny class of developers and frontier models only.

Gap: Section 22757.12 requires only large frontier developers (as defined in CA-SB53-22757-11) to review and update their frontier AI framework at least once a year and to publish material modifications with justification within 30 days; it covers a catastrophic-risk framework, not the suitability, adequacy and effectiveness of a whole management system, and most organisations are out of scope.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework with version history; annual framework review record; published material-change justification (within 30 days)
Rationale: Section 22757.12 is the only California provision imposing a recurring review-and-update cycle, so it is the genuine counterpart to continual improvement, but its scope is narrow (large frontier developers, catastrophic-risk framework only).

Gap: Section 22757.13 requires frontier developers to report critical safety incidents to the Office of Emergency Services within 15 days (24 hours where there is imminent risk of death or serious physical injury); it is a reporting duty only, with no root-cause analysis, no corrective-action or recurrence-prevention process, and no verification that a fix worked, and it applies only to frontier developers (models over 10^26 operations).
Evidence_Examples: Critical safety incident reports to the Office of Emergency Services (15-day / 24-hour); incident response records; amended incident reports
Rationale: Section 22757.13 is the closest California counterpart because it forces a documented response to the most serious nonconformities, but reporting an incident is not the same as correcting it, finding its cause and preventing recurrence.

Gap: Large frontier developers only (as defined in CA-SB53-22757-11); the frontier AI framework is a published transparency document, not a full AIMS covering all AI activities.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; annual framework review and update record; pre-deployment transparency report
Rationale: Section 22757.12 requires a large frontier developer to write, implement, comply with and publish a frontier AI framework and review it at least annually, which partly evidences a maintained governance system, but only for the narrow frontier-developer class.

Gap: Applies only to large frontier developers (as defined in CA-SB53-22757-11) and to frontier models. A published framework and transparency report are not top-management ownership, resourcing, or integration of governance into business processes for all AI use. In force 1 Jan 2026.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; annual framework review/update record; pre-deployment transparency report
Rationale: Section 22757.12 requires large frontier developers to write, implement and publish a frontier AI framework and transparency reports, which requires the developer organisation to own documented commitments, but the statute imposes no top-management commitment, resourcing or integration duty, so the overlap is partial and narrow.

Gap: The frontier AI framework is a published document describing the developer's approach to catastrophic-risk assessment and mitigation, but only for large frontier developers and frontier models. It does not require a general AI policy covering all AI use, framing objectives, or distribution to all who need it.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; pre-deployment transparency report; annual framework review record
Rationale: Section 22757.12's published frontier AI framework is the closest California counterpart to a documented AI policy, but its scope is limited to frontier models of large developers.

Gap: Applies only to large frontier developers (as defined in CA-SB53-22757-11) and only to catastrophic risk; it does not require organisation-wide planning for all AI risks and opportunities.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; annual framework review record; catastrophic-risk assessment summary
Rationale: The frontier AI framework is a documented plan to manage, assess and mitigate catastrophic risks, which partly evidences planned risk action, but only for a narrow class of developers and risks.

Gap: Applies only to large frontier developers and only to catastrophic risk (death or serious injury to over 50 people or over $1B damage); it is not a general AI risk assessment method for all systems and risks.
Evidence_Examples: Frontier AI framework; catastrophic-risk assessment summary in the transparency report; third-party evaluator report
Rationale: The framework must describe how the developer assesses catastrophic-risk capability and applies mitigations, which partly evidences risk assessment, but only for frontier models and catastrophic risk.

Gap: Applies only to large frontier developers and only to mitigation of catastrophic risk; it does not require treatment decisions, owners, or residual-risk records for general AI risks.
Evidence_Examples: Frontier AI framework mitigation section; catastrophic-risk assessment with mitigations; incident-response record
Rationale: The framework must describe mitigation strategies for catastrophic risk, which partly evidences risk treatment, but only for frontier models and catastrophic risk.

Gap: The frontier AI framework describes how a large frontier developer approaches catastrophic-risk management, but the Act sets no measurable AI objectives and no planning duty covering owners, resources, deadlines or evaluation criteria.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; annual framework review record
Rationale: The closest related requirement is the frontier AI framework, a planning document for catastrophic risk only; it does not satisfy measurable AI objectives and achievement planning, so this is recorded as None.

Gap: Section 22757.12(b) requires annual review of the frontier AI framework and publication of material modifications with justification within 30 days, but only for a large frontier developer's framework, not planned and controlled change to the management system.
Evidence_Examples: Annual frontier AI framework review record; published material-modification notice with justification
Rationale: The closest related requirement is the framework review and modification-publication duty, which governs changes to one document for frontier developers only, not management-system change control, so this is recorded as None.

Gap: §22757.12 imposes no duty to determine or provide resources for a management system. The only nearby hook is §22757.12(a)(9), which requires the framework to describe internal governance practices to ensure the framework is implemented — a description topic inside the framework document, not a resourcing duty — and it binds only large frontier developers.
Evidence_Examples: Frontier AI framework implementation plan (shows the gap: a plan to implement a document, not a resourcing duty); resourcing and budget records (voluntary under the Act, not required by it); governance meeting records
Rationale: §22757.12 requires the framework to be written, implemented and complied with and to describe internal governance practices under (a)(9), but it sets no resourcing duty; implementing a document does not by itself evidence provision of management-system resources, so there is no counterpart.

Gap: The frontier AI framework duty binds large frontier developers only (as defined in CA-SB53-22757-11) and addresses catastrophic risk only; no general operational planning for other AI systems.
Evidence_Examples: Published frontier AI framework; annual framework review record; deployment transparency report
Rationale: Section 22757.12 requires a documented operational protocol for managing, assessing and mitigating catastrophic risk.

Gap: Assessments address catastrophic-risk thresholds for frontier models only, for large frontier developers; no per-system periodic AI risk assessment for general AI, and transparency-report summaries are disclosure, not retained assessment records.
Evidence_Examples: Catastrophic-risk assessment summary in transparency report; threshold definition and assessment record; third-party evaluator involvement record
Rationale: Section 22757.12 requires defining and assessing capability thresholds and publishing assessment summaries.

Gap: Mitigations address catastrophic risk of frontier models for large frontier developers only; no general per-system treatment plan or outcome records; effectiveness assessment is framework-level, not per-treatment outcome records.
Evidence_Examples: Frontier AI framework mitigation section; mitigation effectiveness assessment record; transparency-report mitigation summary
Rationale: Section 22757.12(a)(3) requires applying mitigations based on assessment results.

Gap: Section 22757.12 requires a large frontier developer to review and update its frontier AI framework at least once per year and to publish transparency reports, but this is an annual framework review for frontier developers only, not ongoing monitoring and measurement of management-system performance.
Evidence_Examples: Annual frontier AI framework review record; published transparency reports; framework update log
Rationale: The annual framework review is the closest California duty to performance evaluation, but its scope is limited to large frontier developers and to the safety framework, so the match is partial.

Gap: Section 22757.12 requires a large frontier developer to review and update its frontier AI framework at least once per year, but that is a framework review, not a top-management review of the whole management system, and it applies only to large frontier developers.
Evidence_Examples: Annual framework review record with management sign-off; framework update log
Rationale: The annual framework review is the closest California analogue to a planned management review, but it lacks the top-management suitability, adequacy, and effectiveness determination, so the match is partial.

Gap: The mechanism is a contact route for a natural person to reach the developer, included in the transparency report; it is not a general external problem-reporting channel, and it exists only for frontier developers and only in that report.
Evidence_Examples: Transparency report contact mechanism; developer website contact route; record of communications received
Rationale: §22757.12(c)(1)(B) requires the transparency report to include a mechanism enabling a natural person to communicate with the frontier developer, the closest analogue to an external reporting channel, limited to that single contact route.

Gap: The notice duty covers disclosure rights only, for covered employees of frontier developers; it imposes no general AI awareness duty for all staff.
Evidence_Examples: Workplace posting of disclosure rights; annual written notice with acknowledgement receipt; notice to new and remote employees
Rationale: §1107.1(d) requires continuous workplace posting, with equivalent notice to new and remote employees, or annual written notice with receipt acknowledged, which partly evidences awareness-raising for covered employees, limited to whistleblower rights. Lab. Code text verified via the public.law mirror, not a direct leginfo read (U-02).

Gap: §22757.11 only defines catastrophic risk, frontier model, frontier developer and large frontier developer; it imposes no duty to assess societal impacts.
Evidence_Examples: No artefact exists under this section; a societal-impact assessment record would evidence the control itself
Rationale: The definitions set the scope thresholds that other sections use, including the catastrophic-risk definition in §22757.11(c), but a definition imposes no assessment duty, so there is no counterpart.

Gap: §22757.11 defines the frontier-model threshold (more than 10^26 operations) and catastrophic risk but requires no risk assessment; the assessment duties sit in §22757.12.
Evidence_Examples: No artefact exists under this section; a catastrophic-risk assessment record would evidence the control itself
Rationale: Definitions set the trigger for the assessment duties in §22757.12, but a definition is not an assessment duty, so there is no counterpart.

Gap: The summaries are confidential transmittals to CalOES every three months, not retained per-system assessment records; the duty binds large frontier developers only and covers internal use of frontier models only.
Evidence_Examples: Quarterly internal-use catastrophic-risk assessment summary transmitted to CalOES; internal-use assessment record; transmittal schedule communicated in writing
Rationale: §22757.12(d) requires large developers to transmit summaries of catastrophic-risk assessments from internal use, which partly evidences periodic AI risk assessment, limited to internal use and to summary transmittal rather than retained assessment records.

Gap: The summaries go confidentially to CalOES, not to interested parties generally; §22757.12(d) imposes no public sharing duty.
Evidence_Examples: No artefact exists under this section for interested-party sharing; the confidential CalOES transmittal record shows the gap
Rationale: The (d) duty is a confidential regulatory transmittal, the opposite of sharing information with interested parties, so there is no counterpart.

Gap: The (d) summary is a confidential transmittal to CalOES, not technical documentation supplied to relevant parties for an AI system.
Evidence_Examples: No artefact exists under this section; the published framework and transparency report evidence the control itself under §22757.12(a)-(c)
Rationale: A confidential summary sent to a regulator is not technical documentation for relevant parties, so there is no counterpart.

Gap: Section 22757.12(e) is a ban on materially false or misleading statements, not an affirmative duty to share accurate information with interested parties; for framework implementation and compliance statements it binds large frontier developers only.
Evidence_Examples: Published framework and transparency report statements; statement review record; redaction justification log
Rationale: §22757.12(e) bans materially false or misleading statements about catastrophic risk and framework compliance, which partly overlaps truthful communication with interested parties, but only as a negative duty.

Gap: Redactions shape what is published in the framework and transparency report, but the five-year retention of unredacted material has no technical-documentation counterpart, and (f) imposes no documentation content duty of its own.
Evidence_Examples: Published framework and transparency report with stated redaction character and justification; retained unredacted material (five years)
Rationale: §22757.12(f) allows redactions with stated justification and requires five-year retention of unredacted material, which partly overlaps technical documentation practice for published frontier-model documents.

Gap: §22757.15 is an enforcement consequence (an AG civil penalty of up to $1M per violation); it requires no root-cause analysis, corrective action or recurrence prevention.
Evidence_Examples: No artefact exists under this section; a corrective-action record for a framework or reporting failure would evidence the control itself
Rationale: A penalty for failing to publish, report or follow a framework creates an incentive to comply but imposes no nonconformity correction process, so there is no counterpart.

Gap: §22757.15 imposes a penalty, not a duty to review or improve a management system; no continual-improvement cycle is required.
Evidence_Examples: No artefact exists under this section; a framework review and improvement record would evidence the control itself
Rationale: An enforcement penalty is a consequence for non-compliance, not a continual-improvement duty, so there is no counterpart.

Gap: High-level summary of training datasets covering at least 12 items per §3111(a)(1)–(12) (sources or owners, intended purpose, data-point counts, types, intellectual-property status, purchased or licensed, personal-information and aggregate consumer-information flags, cleaning or processing and its purpose, collection period, first-use dates, synthetic-data use) for generative AI systems made available to Californians; training data only, not all data resources.
Evidence_Examples: Published training-data documentation on the developer website; dataset summary records; data collection-period logs
Rationale: Civil Code section 3111 is the closest California counterpart because it requires training-data documentation to be published, but it is a high-level summary of training data, not a full data-resource record.

Gap: AB 2013 (Civ. Code s. 3111) requires developers of generative AI systems made publicly available to Californians to post training-data documentation covering at least 12 items, including dataset sources, types and collection period, but this covers only training data, not design and development choices generally, and only for generative AI.
Evidence_Examples: Published training-data documentation (s. 3111 12-item minimum summary); dataset sources and provenance log; substantial-modification update record
Rationale: AB 2013 s. 3111 is a genuine design-documentation duty for one input (training data) for generative AI, so it partially covers A.6.2.3 for that slice only.

Gap: AB 2013 (Civ. Code s. 3111) requires public posting of training-data documentation for generative AI systems, but this is one documentation topic for one audience (the public), not the technical documentation each relevant party needs.
Evidence_Examples: Published training-data documentation; dataset provenance log; substantial-modification update record
Rationale: AB 2013 s. 3111 is a genuine public technical-documentation duty for training data, which partially covers A.6.2.7 for that topic and audience only.

Gap: Civil Code 3111 requires a developer of a generative AI system/service to post public documentation on training data (12-item minimum summary) before public availability; it is a public disclosure duty for generative AI only, not an internal data-management process for all AI development and enhancement.
Evidence_Examples: Published training-data documentation (3111 12-item minimum summary); dataset inventory feeding the disclosure; data-management procedure (no AB 2013 counterpart)
Rationale: Section 3111 is the closest California analogue to data management for development, because its 12-item minimum documentation covers datasets, sources, cleaning and collection periods. It is Partial because it mandates public disclosure, not an internal management process, and covers generative AI only.

Gap: Section 3111(a) requires disclosure of dataset sources/owners, whether datasets were purchased or licensed, and whether they include personal or aggregate consumer information; it discloses sources after the fact and does not require a documented acquisition or selection decision. Generative AI only.
Evidence_Examples: Published 3111 summary (sources/owners, purchased/licensed, personal-information flags); dataset acquisition/licence register; source-selection decision record (no AB 2013 counterpart)
Rationale: Section 3111(a)(1), (6)-(8) require the sources, owners and acquisition mode of training datasets to be published, which is the closest California analogue to acquisition. It is Partial because disclosure of sources is not a documented acquisition/selection process.

Gap: Section 3111(a)(9) requires disclosure of whether cleaning, processing or other modification of datasets occurred and its intended purpose; it does not require the developer to define data-quality requirements or to check that they are met. Generative AI only.
Evidence_Examples: Published 3111 summary (cleaning/processing disclosure); data-quality requirements document (no AB 2013 counterpart); dataset quality check report (no AB 2013 counterpart)
Rationale: Section 3111(a)(9) is the closest California provision touching data quality, because it surfaces cleaning and processing of training data. It is Partial because disclosing the fact and purpose of processing only is not defining quality requirements or verifying them.

Gap: Section 3111(a) requires disclosure of dataset sources/owners, dates datasets were first used, the collection time period (including whether collection is ongoing), and synthetic-data use; it is a high-level public summary for generative AI only and does not require a full lineage or change history per dataset.
Evidence_Examples: Published 3111 summary (sources, first-use dates, collection period, synthetic-data flag); dataset provenance register; dataset version/change log (no AB 2013 counterpart)
Rationale: Section 3111 is the closest California analogue for data provenance, because it requires sources, first-use dates and collection periods to be published. It is Partial because a high-level summary is not a provenance chain recording how data changed over time.

Gap: Section 3111(a)(9) requires disclosure of whether there was any cleaning, processing or other modification of datasets and the intended purpose of those alterations; it discloses that preparation happened, but does not require documented preparation criteria or methods. Generative AI only.
Evidence_Examples: Published 3111 summary (cleaning/processing disclosure); data-preparation procedure (no AB 2013 counterpart); preparation run log per dataset (no AB 2013 counterpart)
Rationale: Section 3111(a)(9) expressly covers cleaning, processing or other modification of training datasets, making it the closest California analogue to A.7.6. It is Partial because the duty is to disclose the fact and purpose of alterations, not to define and document preparation criteria and methods.

Gap: Section 3111 requires developers of GenAI systems or services to post training-data documentation on their website, but the duty covers training-data facts only and gives no instructions on how to use the system. The sole overlap with this control is the public-posting channel (the developer website); §3111 contributes nothing to user information, so there is no substantive coverage.
Evidence_Examples: Published training-data documentation page on the developer website (training-data facts only; no user instructions); dataset summary records; version history of the published documentation
Rationale: Section 3111 shares only the public-posting channel with this control: it publishes training-data facts on the developer website but provides no user information or instructions on how to use the system, so the match is None.

Gap: Section 3111 requires developers of GenAI systems or services to post training-data documentation on their website, making defined information available to the public and other interested parties, but only for GenAI released on or after 1 Jan 2022 and only about training data, not about the system's operation, risks, or incidents.
Evidence_Examples: Published training-data documentation page; dataset summary records; version history of the published documentation
Rationale: Section 3111 is mapped separately from SB 53 because it is a public information-sharing duty applying to GenAI developers generally, but its subject is training data only, so it is Partial for A.8.5.

Gap: Civil Code 3111 requires developers to post training-data documentation covering at least 12 items on their website before a generative AI system or service (or substantial modification) is made publicly available to Californians; it is a single prescribed document set, not the full management-system documented information 7.5.1 requires.
Evidence_Examples: Published training-data documentation; documented-information index; posting and version records
Rationale: Section 3111 is the California documented-information duty, but it covers training-data documentation only, so Partial.

Gap: Civil Code 3111 requires documentation to be posted before each substantial modification is made publicly available, which forces a re-posting trigger, but prescribes no identification, format, review or approval controls for creating and updating documents. A timing trigger alone is not a document-control process, so there is no substantive coverage.
Evidence_Examples: Document approval records (no AB 2013 counterpart); version-controlled documentation (no AB 2013 counterpart); pre-release checklist (no AB 2013 counterpart)
Rationale: Section 3111 creates an update trigger tied to each release, but an update trigger is not a document creation and update control process, so the match is None.

Gap: Risk-assessment duty only: s.7150 requires assessment before processing that triggers it (including using ADMT for a significant decision); it does not require the AI policy to be checked against privacy, security or quality policies, and reaches only CCPA-covered businesses whose processing meets a s.7150(b) trigger, which also covers selling or sharing personal information, processing sensitive personal information and automated profiling inferences, not only ADMT for significant decisions. Risk assessments are required before initiation from 1 Jan 2026; 31 Dec 2027 is only the backfill deadline for processing begun before 1 Jan 2026.
Evidence_Examples: CCPA risk assessment covering ADMT use; assessment record linking AI policy to privacy controls
Rationale: CCPA Regs s.7150 makes ADMT use for a significant decision a risk-assessment trigger, so an assessment partly evidences the AI policy being checked against privacy duties, but it is a processing risk assessment, not a policy-alignment check.

Gap: §7150 triggers a risk assessment only before processing that presents significant privacy risk (including using ADMT for a significant decision or training ADMT for one); it is a privacy-risk trigger, not a general process to assess consequences of AI systems for people and society, and applies only to covered CCPA businesses.
Evidence_Examples: Risk-assessment trigger checklist per processing activity; ADMT significant-decision determinations; §7150(b) trigger log
Rationale: §7150 is the closest California analogue to an impact-assessment process: it compels an assessment before specified ADMT processing begins, but its privacy-only scope and covered-business threshold leave most A.5.2 systems outside it.

Gap: §7152 requires a documented risk-assessment report, but only for privacy risks of the processing in §7150, not for impact-assessment results generally; retention and review timing sit in §7155 (review at least every three years, update within 45 days of a material change, retain while processing continues or five years after completion, whichever is later).
Evidence_Examples: Risk-assessment report per §7152(a) (purpose, data, ADMT logic, benefits, negative impacts, safeguards, reviewer approval); §7155 review/update log; CPPA submission record under §7157
Rationale: §7152 prescribes the documented, approved report A.5.3 wants — including negative impacts, safeguards and sign-off — but only for CCPA privacy-risk assessments, so an organisation's wider IA results are not covered by the duty.

Gap: §7152(a)(5) requires negative impacts on consumers' privacy, with sources and causes, and §7152(a)(3)(G) the ADMT logic, assumptions and limitations, but that logic item applies only to §7150(b)(3) uses (ADMT for a significant decision) and not to training-only assessments; the lens is individual consumer privacy only; there is no required assessment of fairness or safety effects on individuals or groups, and no group-level analysis.
Evidence_Examples: Risk-assessment report sections on negative privacy impacts and ADMT logic; stakeholder-involvement record under §7151; consumer complaint log
Rationale: The §7152 report is the strongest California evidence of a documented per-system impact analysis, and its negative-impact and ADMT-logic contents overlap A.5.4, but it is privacy-scoped and individual-consumer framed, so fairness and safety effects on groups are unassessed.

Gap: §7150/§7152 risk assessments weigh privacy risks against benefits to the consumer, business, other stakeholders and the public, and §7154 states the goal of restricting or prohibiting processing if privacy risks outweigh benefits — it states a goal and does not itself bar processing (the proceed decision is recorded under §7152(a)(7)) — but the balancing is privacy-risk only, for covered CCPA businesses, and is not an assessment of wider societal effects.
Evidence_Examples: Risk-assessment report with benefits/negative-impact balancing; §7154 go/no-go decision record; stakeholder-involvement record under §7151
Rationale: The CCPA risk assessment's benefits-versus-risks balancing, including benefits to the public, is a fragment of societal-impact thinking, but it is confined to privacy risk of a processing activity and cannot carry A.5.5's wider societal assessment.

Gap: CCPA ADMT regulations (11 CCR s. 7150, Art. 10) require a risk assessment before using ADMT for a significant decision, but they impose no ongoing operation or monitoring duty for the system in use; the assessment itself must be reviewed at least every three years and updated within 45 days of a material change (s.7155), which is an assessment review cycle, not system monitoring. Evidence_Examples: Risk assessment for the ADMT use (s. 7150); pre-use notice record (s. 7220); opt-out/human-appeal log (s. 7221)

Rationale: Section 7150(b)(6) is a distinct California hook for data used in development: it forces assessment before training ADMT on personal information, and 'intends to use' is defined broadly to include permitting others to use and advertising or marketing the use. Gap: The section 7150 risk assessment is a privacy risk assessment for specified processing, including ADMT for a significant decision; it assesses privacy harms (including discrimination and economic harm) but is not a full AI system impact assessment covering individuals, groups and society.

Rationale: Section 7150 requires identifying negative impacts to consumers' privacy and safeguards before ADMT use, which partly evidences impact assessment, but only for privacy risk in the CCPA setting.

Rationale: Section 7220 is a consumer-notice duty, not a staff-awareness duty, so the match is None. Re-read in full from the official text and confirmed, 21 Nov 2026.

Gap: 11 CCR 7220 prescribes a specific consumer notice (purpose, opt-out or appeal, access right, non-retaliation, how the ADMT works) at or before collection; it does not require a general internal and external management-system communication plan. Rationale: Section 7150 is California's closest pre-use assessment duty.

Rationale: The 7150 assessment is California's closest pre-use impact-oriented assessment.

Rationale: Section 7157 prescribes a documented, attested submission of risk-assessment information, which partly evidences documented assessment reporting, but only for CCPA privacy-risk assessments and only as a filing to the regulator.

Gap: The s.7157 submission is an annual filing of risk-assessment information to the regulator; it evidences that assessments were conducted, but it evaluates no management-system performance and applies only to CCPA-covered businesses.

Rationale: The yearly submission cycle is a periodic, regulator-facing check that risk assessments were conducted, a fragment of monitoring and evaluation, but its object is assessment completion, not management-system performance.

Gap: Section 7221 gives consumers a choice about ADMT use for a significant decision, but only for CCPA-covered businesses and only for significant decisions; it is an opt-out mechanism, not general user information about an AI system.
Evidence_Examples: Opt-out submission methods and confirmation records; pre-use notice stating the opt-out right (s.7220)
Rationale: The opt-out right and its confirmation are user-facing information and choice about an AI system being used on the consumer, which partly overlaps a user-information duty, but it is confined to significant decisions under the CCPA. Re-read in full from the official text and confirmed, 21 Nov 2026, including the 12-month re-ask rule, §7221(k).

Gap: Section 7221 gives consumers an opt-out choice, but it imposes no duty to take customer needs and expectations into account; choice at the point of use is not a needs-and-expectations process.

Rationale: The opt-out mechanism is consumer choice, not a process for identifying or addressing customer needs and expectations, so the match is None. Re-read in full from the official text and confirmed, 21 Nov 2026, including the 12-month re-ask rule, §7221(k).

Gap: Section 7222 requires a plain-language explanation of purpose, ADMT logic and outcome, but only for CCPA-covered businesses using ADMT for a significant decision and only on request; it is not general user information about an AI system.
Evidence_Examples: Access-request responses explaining ADMT purpose, logic and outcome; access-request log
Rationale: The access explanation gives the affected consumer information about how the technology processed their personal information and how the output was used, which partly overlaps a user-information duty, but it is request-driven and confined to significant decisions. Re-read in full from the official text and confirmed, 21 Nov 2026, including the aggregate-response rule, §7222(j), and Article 5 timing, §7021.

Gap: Section 7222 prescribes a specific consumer communication (the access explanation) with Article 5 timing; it does not require a general internal and external management-system communication plan.
Evidence_Examples: Access-request response records; acknowledgement and response-timing log
Rationale: The access response is a prescribed external communication about ADMT use, a fragment of a communication duty, but it is one consumer response rather than a communication plan. Re-read in full from the official text and confirmed, 21 Nov 2026, including the aggregate-response rule, §7222(j), and Article 5 timing, §7021.

Gap: Section 7153 requires a business making ADMT available to another business to hand over facts the recipient needs for its own risk assessment; it supports a risk assessment but prescribes no assessment method, and it applies only to ADMT trained using personal information and only where the recipient uses it for a significant decision.
Evidence_Examples: Facts package provided to the recipient business; recipient risk-assessment record referencing the supplied facts
Rationale: The facts duty feeds the recipient's risk assessment directly, so it partly overlaps a risk-assessment process, but the duty sits on the supplying business as a disclosure obligation, not on the assessment method itself.

Gap: The s.7120-7123 cybersecurity audit is a periodic evaluation, but its object is the business's cybersecurity program and its protection of personal information, not AI management-system performance; it applies only to businesses meeting the s.7120(b) significant-security-risk test.
Evidence_Examples: Annual cybersecurity audit report (s.7123); audit-period record; remediation plan with timeframes
Rationale: An annual, evidence-based audit with a report to an executive is a periodic evaluation mechanism, but it evaluates a cybersecurity program, not an AI management system, so the match is partial.

Gap: The s.7123 audit report describes the program assessed, gaps and a remediation plan and goes to an executive with cybersecurity-program responsibility, which supplies structured material that could feed a review, but no management-review input set is defined and the content serves cybersecurity governance, not a management review of an AI system.
Evidence_Examples: Cybersecurity audit report (program description, gaps, remediation plan); executive receipt record
Rationale: The audit report's structured contents — program assessed, criteria, evidence, gaps, remediation plan — are the closest California source of review inputs from the audit, but they are not a defined management-review input list.

Gap: Section 7124 requires an annual written certification that the cybersecurity audit was completed, but the certification attests completion only; it evaluates no management-system performance and applies only to businesses required to audit under Article 9.
Evidence_Examples: Annual s.7124 certification of completion (business name, point of contact, period covered, executive attestation); audit completion record
Rationale: The yearly certification is a periodic, attested confirmation that an evaluation (the audit) was completed, a fragment of monitoring and evaluation, but it certifies completion of a cybersecurity audit, not management-system performance.

Gap: Section 7124 certifies that a cybersecurity audit was completed; it documents no impact-assessment result and requires no assessment contents, so there is no overlap with documented impact-assessment reporting beyond the fact that both involve a written record.
Evidence_Examples: No applicable evidence: the certification attests audit completion only and contains no impact-assessment content.
Rationale: A completion certificate is not an impact-assessment record, so the match is None.

Gap: A.4.5 concerns documenting the systems and computing resources an AI system relies on. Section 22757.3 requires a latent disclosure naming the provider, the system name and version, the time and date of creation or alteration, a unique identifier, whether the system created or altered the content and, from 1 Jan 2029, whether it is designed primarily as assistive technology, in content created or altered except by minor modification and only to the extent technically feasible, and requires the disclosure to be permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove or tamper with, compatible with the provider's disclosure verification tool, and compliant or interoperable with widely recognized industry standards. Naming the system and version in output content documents no computing resources or dependencies, so the control is unaddressed by this section; the only overlap is the system name, which is not the control's substance.
Evidence_Examples: No artifact arises under this section for computing resources; a voluntary system and computing-resource inventory with dependency records would evidence the control.
Rationale: Section 22757.3 was mapped here because its latent disclosure names the system and version, but the control's substance is computing resources and dependencies, which the section never addresses; the match is None, not Partial.

Gap: Section 22757.3(a), as amended by SB 1000, requires a covered provider, to the extent technically feasible, to include a latent disclosure in image, video or audio content created or altered, except by minor modification, conveying the provider name, system name and version, creation or alteration time and date, a unique identifier, whether the system created or altered the content and, from 1 Jan 2029, whether it is designed primarily as assistive technology; the disclosure must be permanent or extraordinarily difficult to remove or tamper with, compatible with the provider's disclosure verification tool, and compliant or interoperable with widely recognized industry standards. This is provenance of AI-generated OUTPUT, captured as metadata that travels with the content and can be read back through the §22757.2 tool - a genuine partial overlap with A.7.5's provenance-metadata practice - but it is not provenance of the training data, so it does not satisfy A.7.5. SB 1000 removed the 1,000,000-user threshold and the manifest-disclosure option.
Evidence_Examples: Latent-disclosure (watermark/provenance metadata) specification; output provenance record; disclosure verification tool output showing provenance data
Rationale: Section 22757.3 is a distinct California provenance requirement, but for generated content rather than training data. It is mapped as a Partial row because output provenance is materially different from training-data provenance and does not satisfy A.7.5.

Gap: SB 1000 deleted the manifest (visible) disclosure, which was the closest user-facing element for A.8.2 (system documentation and information for users). What remains under §22757.3 is a machine-readable latent disclosure embedded in generated or altered content - content provenance, not documentation explaining the system to users - and it binds generative AI providers only. The only user-facing sliver is the system identity recoverable from content through the §22757.2 disclosure verification tool, and that belongs to the §22757.2 requirement, not this section. Section 22757.3 therefore does not address A.8.2.
Evidence_Examples: No user-facing system documentation arises under this section; latent disclosure metadata in generated content (shows the gap: machine-readable content marking, not user documentation); a user guide or system information notice would evidence the control.
Rationale: Section 22757.3 was mapped here as the closest California analogue for telling users content is AI-generated, but a latent disclosure is provenance marking of outputs, not user-facing system documentation, and the visible-disclosure option that supplied the user-facing element was deleted by SB 1000; the match is None.

Gap: As amended by SB 1000 (30 Sep 2026), §22757.3(b)(2)-(4) requires a covered provider that knows an identifiable licensee modified a licensed generative AI system so it no longer complies to terminate the licensee's authorization or notify the licensee within 72 hours of discovery; the licensee must modify the system to comply or cease using or making available the system (including a copy or modified version), and report which action it took to the provider within 96 hours of receiving the notice - the 96 hours runs on the licensee's report, and the text sets no separate deadline for the fix or cessation itself. If no report arrives, or the report shows the licensee did neither, the provider must report the licensee's noncompliance to the Attorney General, and that report carries no statutory deadline. The provider must also notify a licensee of its chapter obligations when granting the license, and has no duty to monitor, investigate or inquire into licensee use or modification, which limits the evidence a provider can be expected to hold. (The 72-hour, 96-hour and Attorney General-report duties sit in subdivision (b), not (c); subdivision (c) only requires the Attorney General to establish a mechanism to receive the reports.) This is a provider-to-regulator duty about licensee noncompliance, not a channel for outside parties to report problems with the system, so it addresses A.8.3 only in part.
Evidence_Examples: Licensee noncompliance notices and 72-hour terminate-or-notify records; Attorney General reports on noncompliant licensees; license terms requiring disclosure compliance
Rationale: Section 22757.3 is mapped separately for A.8.3 because its licensee-reporting duty is a distinct reporting obligation, but it is a narrow provider-to-regulator duty, not a general external reporting channel.

Gap: Section 22757.2 requires a covered provider to supply a free disclosure verification tool that outputs any system provenance data detected in content and lets a user assess whether the content was created or altered by the provider's system. The tool's personal-information limits and feedback duty do not add provenance coverage.
Evidence_Examples: Disclosure verification tool specification and test records; tool output showing detected system provenance data; user feedback log on tool efficacy
Rationale: Section 22757.2 is mapped to A.7.5 because the tool's core function is detecting and surfacing provenance data, which overlaps with data-provenance practice for outputs, while remaining distinct from training-data provenance.

Gap: The §22757.2 tool is a user-facing verification service: it lets a user check whether a particular item of content was created or altered by the provider's system and shows detected system provenance data. It supplies no documentation or information explaining the system itself - its capabilities, limitations, intended use or operation - to users, which is the substance of A.8.2. The tool answers a question about individual content, not about the system, so it does not address the control.
Evidence_Examples: No system documentation arises under this section; tool user-interface copy and help text (shows the gap: content-checking instructions, not system documentation); a user guide or system information notice would evidence the control.
Rationale: Section 22757.2 was considered for A.8.2 because the tool is user-facing, but user-facing verification of individual content is not system documentation or information for users; the match is None.

Gap: Section 22757.3.1, as rewritten by AB 2713, requires a large online platform to detect provenance data in distributed content, to show users through its interface whether system provenance data or a digital signature identifies content as generated or substantially altered by a generative AI system or captured by a capture device, and to let users inspect system provenance data via the interface, a link or a download. Detecting, surfacing and exposing provenance metadata is a genuine partial overlap with A.7.5's provenance practice, but the platform surfaces provenance of DISTRIBUTED content, not provenance of the training data behind any system, and it creates no provenance record of its own, so it does not satisfy A.7.5. Rationale: Section 22757.3.1 is mapped to A.7.5 because the platform's detection, display and inspection duties all turn on provenance data, overlapping with data-provenance practice for content, while remaining distinct from training-data provenance.

Gap: Section 22757.3.1, as rewritten by AB 2713, requires a large online platform's user interface to reliably indicate whether content is generated or substantially altered by a generative AI system or captured by a capture device, and to make clearly and conspicuously available information sufficient to identify the content's authenticity, origin or history of modification. That is genuinely user-facing information, and it is the strongest user-facing element in the chapter - but it is information about individual items of distributed content, not documentation explaining a generative AI system to its users, and the duty falls on the platform, not on the provider of the system that generated the content. It therefore addresses A.8.2 only in part.
Evidence_Examples: Platform user-interface specification for provenance indicators; content authenticity, origin and modification-history displays; user-facing provenance information notices
Rationale: Section 22757.3.1 is mapped to A.8.2 because its interface duties give users information about content provenance, which is one facet of informing users, while stopping short of system documentation.

No user-facing documentation or system information is produced, and the platform's users receive no notice under this section, so it does not address A.8.2.
Evidence_Examples: No user-facing documentation arises under this section; hosting-platform takedown or availability records (shows the gap: enforcement records, not user information)
Rationale: Section 22757.3.2 was considered for A.8.2 because hosting platforms serve users, but the section imposes a silent availability ban with no information duty; the match is None.

Rationale: Section 22757.3.3 is mapped to A.7.5 because the device-embedded latent disclosure creates content provenance metadata, overlapping with data-provenance practice for captured content, while remaining distinct from training-data provenance.

Rationale: Section 22757.3.3 was considered for A.4.5 because its latent disclosure names the device and version, but the control's substance is computing resources and dependencies, which the section never addresses; the match is None.

Evidence_Examples: No reporting channel arises under this section; civil penalty action records (shows the gap: enforcement records, not an external reporting channel)
Rationale: Section 22757.4.1 was considered for A.8.3 because enforcement involves the Attorney General, but a civil penalty action by a public enforcer is not an external reporting channel; the match is None.

Gap: Section 11017 requires a job-related and business-necessity showing only when a selection device, including an automated-decision system, has adverse impact; it imposes no freestanding duty to assess fairness, privacy or safety impacts on individuals or groups, and the regime covers employment selection only.
Evidence_Examples: Adverse-impact analyses by protected class; business-necessity documentation and validation studies for the selection ADS; records of less-discriminatory alternatives considered
Rationale: FEHA's adverse-impact framework is the California regime that most directly probes discriminatory impact on groups of individuals, and an impact assessment of the selection system is the practical way to produce the business-necessity showing section 11017 requires — but section 11017 creates a defence burden, not an impact-assessment duty, and it does not cover privacy or safety.

Gap: Employment only: section 11008 treats a person acting as the employer's agent (including administering an ADS) as an employer for FEHA purposes; it does not allocate responsibilities among organisation, partners, suppliers and customers across the AI lifecycle.
Evidence_Examples: Vendor/agent agreements designating FEHA responsibility; ADS vendor administration contracts; record of agent-as-employer determinations
Rationale: Section 11008's agent definition is California's closest responsibility-allocation text for third parties - an agent operating an ADS counts as the employer - but it is a deeming rule inside employment discrimination law, not a lifecycle allocation.

Gap: Employment ADS only; no organisation-wide AIMS scope covering all AI systems, activities and locations.
Evidence_Examples: ADS inventory for employment tools with 11008.1(a) scope assessment per tool; record of tools excluded as non-ADS (e.g. word processing, spreadsheets)
Rationale: Section 11008.1(a) defines an automated-decision system in employment, which lets an employer determine which tools fall in scope, but the boundary is confined to employment decisions. ISO 4.3 scope confirmed from Advisera, ISO 42001 Mandatory Documents (checked 2026-11-21).

Gap: Section 11009(f) states a non-discrimination prohibition and an evidentiary rule: evidence, or the lack of it, of anti-bias testing is relevant to a discrimination claim. It imposes no duty to carry out an impact assessment of any kind, so an impact-assessment process does not satisfy, even in part, anything section 11009(f) requires; the overlap is thematic (discriminatory impact) only, and the regime covers employment automated-decision systems only.
Evidence_Examples: Anti-bias testing report (quality, efficacy, recency, scope); test results and response record
Rationale: Clause 6.1.4 is an AI system impact-assessment process; section 11009(f) imposes no impact-assessment duty at all, so there is no partial satisfaction to record — the thematic overlap with discriminatory impact does not make the control a partial implementation of the requirement.

Gap: 2 CCR 11013(c) requires employers to preserve personnel and employment records, expressly including automated-decision system data, for at least four years from the later of the record date or the personnel action; it sets retention only, with no access, distribution, storage or versioning control for management-system documented information generally.
Evidence_Examples: Retention schedule (four-year); automated-decision system data archive; access log
Rationale: Section 11013(c) is the California retention duty reaching AI-related records, but retention alone is only part of 7.5.3, so Partial. ISO 7.5.3 scope confirmed from iso42001gapassessment.com (checked 2026-11-21).

Gap: Section 1522 bars sole reliance on an ADS for discipline or termination decisions and requires human corroboration where reliance is primary, using the data behind the output or other supporting information; it also bars the prohibited uses in §1522(a) and the use of output that cannot be corroborated or is inaccurate, incomplete or misleading. That is employment discipline and termination only, not a record of human resources and competencies for all AI lifecycle roles, and it sets no competency standard for the corroborating human.
Evidence_Examples: Human-corroboration records citing the data or supporting information relied on, such as supervisor evaluations, personnel files, employee work product, peer reviews or witness interviews; designated corroborator assignments showing who performed each corroboration
Rationale: Labor Code section 1522 is the closest California counterpart because it requires human corroboration where an employer primarily relies on an ADS for a discipline or termination decision, but it governs one employment decision type, not lifecycle-wide human resources.

Gap: Lab. Code §1524 (added by SB 947, operative 1 Jul 2027) requires an employer that primarily relied on an ADS for a disciplinary or termination decision to give the affected employee a written post-use notice at the time the decision is communicated. The notice must be in plain language, a separate stand-alone communication, in the language of routine employee communications, and delivered by a simple easy-to-use method such as email, a hyperlink or another written format. Its contents are the ADS reliance, human corroboration, a contact person for more information about the decision and the data-description right, and that retaliation is prohibited; §1522(b)(2) supplies the human-corroboration duty and §1522(d) the data-description right — but only for discipline/termination decisions and only for employees.
Evidence_Examples: Issued stand-alone plain-language post-use notices in the language of routine employee communications, with delivery method and date recorded; human-corroboration records; employee data-description request responses
Rationale: Section 1524 is a distinct California notice duty because it informs an affected individual after an ADS was used on them, so it maps to A.8.2 separately, but its scope is narrowly employment discipline and termination; the corroboration and data-description elements the notice references sit in §1522(b)(2) and (d).

Gap: Operative 1 Jul 2027 and limited to employment: it bars sole reliance on an ADS for discipline or termination and requires human corroboration of primary reliance, and it bars the prohibited uses in §1522(a), but imposes no general duty to use AI systems as intended or per documentation.
Evidence_Examples: ADS use policy for discipline/termination decisions; human-corroboration records
Rationale: Section 1522 constrains how an ADS may be used in employment decisions - no sole reliance, human corroboration where primarily relied on - which partially mirrors keeping use within intended bounds, but only for one decision type in one context.

Gap: Section 1522(b)(2) requires a human to corroborate a discipline/termination decision where the employer primarily relied on an ADS output — but only for that decision type, only for employers, and only from 1 Jul 2027. It assigns no general AI-governance roles, responsibilities and authorities. The written post-use notice duty sits in §1524, not §1522, and is mapped separately under CA-SB947-1524.
Evidence_Examples: Designated ADS corroboration reviewer assignments; corroboration records citing the data or supporting information relied on
Rationale: Lab. Code §1522 is the closest California role-assignment counterpart: it requires a designated human corroborator for covered ADS employment decisions, but that is a single decision type, not the whole governance system.

Gap: Labor Code 1522 requires human corroboration where an employer primarily relies on automated decision system output for a disciplinary or termination decision, and bars sole reliance; it sets no competence standard, training requirement, or evidence-of-competence requirement for the reviewer or other staff. Operative 1 July 2027.
Evidence_Examples: Control-side artifacts only: role competence matrix; training and qualification records; reviewer appointment records. None of these evidences a §1522 duty, because §1522 sets no competence, training or evidence-of-competence standard.
Rationale: Section 1522 is the closest California hook for staff capability because it requires a human to corroborate, but it requires a human act, not competent staff with evidence, so None.

Gap: Lab. Code §1522 requires human corroboration where an employer primarily relies on an ADS for a disciplinary or termination decision, but that corroboration is a case-level act recorded per decision, not a recorded management-review result; §1522 requires no logging of improvement opportunities or system changes. Operative 1 Jul 2027.
Evidence_Examples: Human-corroboration records; ADS reliance log recording the decision, the ADS output relied on, a primary-reliance flag, the corroborator and the corroboration basis
Rationale: Human corroboration is the closest California analogue to acting on evaluation findings, but it operates per employment decision rather than as a management-review output, so there is no match.

Gap: Lab. Code §1524 requires a written post-use notice to the affected employee at the time a discipline or termination decision is communicated, but that notice is a case-level communication to one employee, not a recorded management-review result; §1524 requires no logging of improvement opportunities or system changes. Operative 1 Jul 2027.
Evidence_Examples: Issued post-use notices; post-use notice log recording the notice date and delivery method
Rationale: The post-use notice is the closest California analogue to acting on evaluation findings, but it operates per employment decision rather than as a management-review output, so there is no match.

Gap: Lab. Code §1526 prohibits an employer from retaliating against an employee for exercising rights under Part 5.5.5, filing a complaint, alleging a violation or cooperating with an investigation. A.8.2 concerns assessing the impact of an AI system on individuals; it sets no non-retaliation protection, no complaint channel and no safeguard for employees who raise concerns, so the anti-retaliation duty has no counterpart here. Operative 1 Jul 2027.
Evidence_Examples: Control-side artifacts only: AI system impact assessment records. No retaliation-protection evidence exists under this control.
Rationale: Section 1526 protects employees who exercise part rights, which is adjacent to assessing impacts on individuals, but it imposes a conduct prohibition rather than an impact-assessment duty, so there is no match.

Gap: Lab. Code §1526 is a prohibition on employer retaliation against employees exercising part rights; it assigns no roles, responsibilities or authorities and requires no designation of who receives or acts on retaliation complaints. Clause 5.3 assigns AI-governance roles but imposes no non-retaliation duty, so the two do not overlap. Operative 1 Jul 2027.
Evidence_Examples: Control-side artifacts only: role and responsibility assignments for AI governance. No retaliation-complaint handling assignment exists under this control.
Rationale: Section 1526 is a conduct prohibition on the employer, not a role-assignment duty, so there is no match with a control about assigning responsibilities.

Gap: Lab. Code §1526 prohibits retaliation against employees exercising part rights; retaliation complaints and investigations are case-level events, not recorded management-review results, and §1526 requires no logging of improvement opportunities or system changes. Operative 1 Jul 2027.
Evidence_Examples: Control-side artifacts only: management-review output records. No retaliation-matter log exists under this control.
Rationale: Retaliation matters are case-level employment events rather than management-review outputs, so there is no match.

Gap: SB 813 does not require the organisation to use a designated independent verification organisation to satisfy its supplier duties, and no designated organisation can exist yet: agency criteria are due 1 Jan 2028 (Executive Order N-9-26 targets 1 May 2027) and no auditor can register before the registry opens 1 Jan 2029 (Executive Order target 1 Dec 2027). The registration bar binds auditors, not the organisation.
Evidence_Examples: Supplier AI assessment records; vendor due-diligence file noting verification-organisation designation or auditor registration status as not yet available; from May 2027 at the earliest, engagement records with a designated verification organisation; from December 2027 at the earliest, engagement records with a registered AI auditor.
Rationale: A.10.3 is Suppliers in ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A (confirmed against public control lists). A designated verification organisation or registered auditor gives the organisation a state-recognised route to check a supplier AI system, but use is voluntary and registration governs who may conduct a covered AI audit, not whether the organisation must assess a supplier. Source: bill status page opened; chaptered text not read from the official source (U-15).
Source_Type: Official URL cited; direct read not confirmed

Gap: Clause 9.2 is an internal, organisation-run audit of its own management system; SB 813's framework is external third-party verification that imposes no internal-audit duty and does not require any developer, deployer, or operator of an AI system to engage a verification organisation or undergo a covered AI audit. The control therefore satisfies no part of the requirement.
Evidence_Examples: Internal audit programme and plan; internal audit reports; corrective-action records. A verification organisation's report is not 9.2 evidence: it is another entity's statutory report, not the organisation's own internal audit.
Rationale: No organisation-side duty exists, so the overlap is analogical only — both involve audits — and internal audit is a different mechanism from external verification. No verification-organisation designation exists until the agency publishes criteria (due 1 Jan 2028; Executive Order N-9-26 targets 1 May 2027). Source: bill status page opened; chaptered text not read from the official source (U-15).
Source_Type: Official URL cited; direct read not confirmed

Gap: AB 1405 imposes no duty on the organisation to engage a registered auditor or to assess a supplier's fit; its only organisation-side consequence is to check that any auditor it engages for a covered AI audit is registered from 1 Jan 2029. No auditor can register before the registry opens on 1 Jan 2029 (Executive Order N-9-26 targets 1 Dec 2027).
Evidence_Examples: Vendor due-diligence file recording an engaged auditor's registration number and a registry check, from 1 Jan 2029; supplier AI assessment records; before the registry opens, a file note recording registration status as not yet available.
Rationale: A.10.3 is Suppliers in ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A (confirmed against public control lists). A registered auditor gives a state-recognised route to verify a supplier AI system, but registration governs who may conduct a covered AI audit, not whether the organisation must assess a supplier; the registration bar binds auditors, not the organisation. Source: law-firm PDF, read 21 Nov 2026; direct read of the official text outstanding (U-16).

Gap: AB 1405 allocates no responsibilities to the organisation: its duties run to the Government Operations Agency (registry) and to auditors (registration and audit duties). Naming an internal owner for checking an engaged auditor's registration is the organisation's own governance choice, not something the chapter requires, so A.10.2 satisfies no part of the requirement.
Evidence_Examples: No evidence can show compliance with this requirement from the organisation's side, because the chapter imposes no duty on it; any internal assignment of a registration-check owner is the organisation's own governance record.
Rationale: A.10.2 is Allocating responsibilities in ISO/IEC 42001:2023 Annex A (confirmed against public control lists). The registry framework allocates responsibilities between the agency and auditors only; it creates no responsibility-allocation duty inside the audited organisation, so the match is nil rather than partial. Source: law-firm PDF, read 21 Nov 2026; direct read of the official text outstanding (U-16).
